passage:
Monday: Mohit Uncle at the corner shop gave Zeenat change for a hundred-rupee note, though she had paid with fifty. Nobody noticed. She walked home with the extra money hot in her pocket.
Tuesday: She kept thinking about it in class. Mohit Uncle always gave her a free toffee. What if he got in trouble with his wife over the money?
Wednesday: After school she went back. "Uncle, you gave me too much on Monday. I knew, and I kept it two days. Sorry." Mohit Uncle blinked, counted, then smiled. "I was short fifty that night and couldn't think why. Thank you, beta."

qa.q: What note had Zeenat actually paid with?
qa.a: She had paid with a fifty-rupee note.

qa.q: What does the money feeling "hot in her pocket" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt guilty about keeping money that wasn't hers.

qa.q: Which choice made Zeenat's week end well?
qa.a: She went back, returned the extra money and admitted she had kept it for two days, even though no one knew.

qa.q: How is Mohit Uncle affected by Zeenat's honesty?
qa.a: He is relieved to solve the missing money and grateful to her.

grounding: It shows a child owning up to keeping extra change and returning it, though no one would have caught her.

passage: "Rukmini, let me tell you about the day I broke Headmaster's window. I was eleven, practising cricket in the empty school ground after class. The ball went straight through the glass. Nobody was there. Nobody saw. I could have just walked home. I sat under the tree for a long time, heart thumping. Then I went to his house and told him. He was angry for a minute. Then he said, 'You came yourself. That matters more than the glass.' I paid for it from my savings. That window taught me more than any lesson." Reena Nani laughed. "Now, what did you want to tell me?"

qa.q: Where was Reena practising cricket?
qa.a: She was practising in the empty school ground after class.

qa.q: What does Reena sitting under the tree with her heart thumping show?
qa.a: It shows she was scared and struggling between hiding it and telling the truth.

qa.q: What might Rukmini take from Reena's story?
qa.a: That owning up even when no one saw is worth more than escaping blame.

qa.q: How might the headmaster have seen Reena after she came to him?
qa.a: He seemed to respect her honesty more than he cared about the broken glass.

grounding: An elder tells a story about admitting a mistake when no one would have caught her.

passage: The lunch bell was about to ring. Lalit was alone in the classroom, rushing to get his tiffin from the shelf, when his elbow hit Rashmi Ma'am's globe. It fell and cracked right across Africa. The corridor was empty. He could put it back with the crack facing the wall. Voices came closer. His hands were sweaty. When Rashmi Ma'am walked in, he blurted, "Ma'am, I broke your globe. I'm sorry." She looked at the crack, then at him. "Thank you for telling me. We'll tape it together after lunch."

qa.q: Where did the globe crack?
qa.a: It cracked right across Africa.

qa.q: What do Lalit's sweaty hands suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he was nervous and tempted to hide the damage.

qa.q: What could Rashmi Ma'am do to encourage more honesty in class?
qa.a: She could thank students like Lalit publicly for owning up and respond calmly to mistakes.

qa.q: What would change if Lalit had hidden the crack?
qa.a: He might have got away with it, but he would carry the guilt and lose his teacher's trust if found out.

grounding: It shows a child admitting a mistake when he could have hidden it, under time pressure.

passage: Asif bhai's stationery shop in the lane behind the Dadar market was packed with parents buying school supplies. Irawati, ten, paid for a geometry box with a hundred-rupee note. He was answering three customers at once and handed her change without looking. On the steps outside, she counted. Too much. He'd given her change for a five hundred. Her heart jumped. Nobody had seen. She could buy the glitter pens. She took four steps toward home. Then she thought of Asif bhai counting his cash box tonight, frowning. She squeezed back through the crowd. 'Bhaiya, you gave me extra.' He stared, then laughed. 'Arre, in this rush! Thank you, beti.'

qa.q: What did Irawati buy at the shop?
qa.a: She bought a geometry box.

qa.q: What made Irawati turn back after four steps?
qa.a: She imagined Asif bhai frowning over his cash box that night and felt it would be wrong to keep money no one knew about.

qa.q: What does Irawati's choice show about acting well when no one is watching?
qa.a: It shows she let her own sense of right, not the fear of being caught, decide what she did.

qa.q: How might Asif bhai see Irawati the next time she visits his shop?
qa.a: He would probably remember her as an honest child and trust her warmly.

grounding: Shows a child returning extra change though she could never have been caught.

passage: 'Mama?' Joseph hovered in the kitchen doorway. Anjali looked up from the dosa pan. 'You're quiet. What happened?' 'When I was cycling in the compound, my pedal scraped Mr D'Costa's scooter. There's a long line now.' 'Did he see?' 'Nobody saw. Nobody was there.' 'So why are you telling me?' Joseph twisted his T-shirt. 'Because it's his scooter. And I keep thinking about it.' Anjali turned off the flame. 'That thinking is your good sense. What do you want to do?' 'Tell him? He'll shout.' 'Maybe. Want me to come?' 'Stand near. But I'll say it.' 'Deal.' They walked down together. Joseph's voice shook, but he said every word.

qa.q: What did Joseph's pedal scrape?
qa.a: It scraped Mr D'Costa's scooter and left a long line.

qa.q: Why did Joseph tell his mother even though nobody saw?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and kept thinking about the damage to someone else's scooter, so he wanted to put it right.

qa.q: How did Anjali support Joseph without taking over?
qa.a: She stayed calm, asked what he wanted to do and offered to stand near while letting him speak for himself.

qa.q: If you were Mr D'Costa, what would you want?
qa.a: You would probably want the truth, and you might be less angry because the boy came himself to admit it.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a mistake no one saw, supported by a parent.

passage:
Last summer, when I was eleven, I was playing cricket alone in the lane and hit the ball into Chandrika-aunty's flower pot. It cracked in two.
Nobody saw. Aunty was at work. I could have just gone home.
I'm Deepak. I stood there for a long time. My stomach felt tight.
When she came home in the evening, I knocked. “Aunty, I broke your pot. I'm sorry.”
She looked at me, then at the pot. “You could have hidden it.”
“I know.”
She laughed and said I could help her repot the tulsi on Sunday. I did. It felt better than hiding.

qa.q: What did Deepak's ball crack?
qa.a: Chandrika-aunty's flower pot.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel standing in the lane after the pot broke?
qa.a: Deepak felt anxious and guilty, with a tight stomach.

qa.q: What choice did Deepak make, and why was it right?
qa.a: Deepak told Chandrika-aunty even though nobody had seen, which was honest and let them fix it together.

qa.q: How did Chandrika-aunty respond to Deepak's honesty?
qa.a: She was surprised, laughed and invited Deepak to help repot the tulsi.

grounding: An eleven-year-old admits breaking a neighbour's pot even though nobody saw.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 6. Ritu Sen.
During Tuesday's maths test, I was called out of the room for five minutes. I left the answer sheet on my desk by mistake.
When I came back, Shalini (eleven) came up to me after the test. She said she'd seen the sheet on my desk. She had turned it face down and had not looked. She was worried others might think she had.
I thanked her. I checked the room and decided to give a new test the next day to be fair.
Shalini's cheeks were pink, but she held her head up.
Next step: I'll keep my papers with me, and I've told Shalini's parents how honest she was.

qa.q: What had the teacher left on the desk?
qa.a: The answer sheet.

qa.q: How was Shalini feeling when she told the teacher?
qa.a: She felt nervous and worried that others might think she had looked.

qa.q: What made Shalini's choice honest?
qa.a: She turned the sheet face down without looking and told the teacher, even though nobody would have known.

qa.q: How might the other students feel about taking a new test?
qa.a: Some may be annoyed, but most may see it as fair.

grounding: A teacher records an eleven-year-old acting honestly when she could not be caught.

passage:
Saturday
I was cycling in the building parking and I scraped the side of a blue car with my pedal. A long white line.
There was nobody there. Not even the watchman.
I stood there for ages. My heart was thumping.
Then I went home and wrote a note: “Sorry, I scratched your car with my cycle. Please call my Mumma.” I wrote her number and taped it to the window.
In the evening Ishita-aunty from the fourth floor rang. Mumma went with me. Aunty said it was only a small scratch and thanked me for owning up.
I thought I'd feel terrible. I actually feel light. — Pema

qa.q: What colour was the car?
qa.a: It was a blue car.

qa.q: How did Pema feel before and after owning up?
qa.a: Pema felt nervous with a thumping heart before, and light and relieved after owning up.

qa.q: Why was writing the note the right choice?
qa.a: It was honest even though nobody saw, and it let the owner decide how to handle it.

qa.q: How did Ishita-aunty react to the note?
qa.a: She said it was a small scratch and thanked Pema for owning up.

grounding: A twelve-year-old admits scratching a car when nobody saw.

passage:
In the market of her small town, Vandana bought a packet of salt from Pema aunty's shop. Pema aunty was busy talking and gave her change for a hundred rupees, but Vandana had given her fifty.
Vandana counted the coins on the way home. Too much. Nobody would ever know. Pema aunty hadn't even looked.
She could buy three ice lollies with it.
She stopped by the tea stall and looked at the coins for a long time. Then she walked back.
"Aunty, you gave me extra." Pema aunty blinked, then laughed. "Arre, I'd have been short tonight! Thank you, beta." She pressed a toffee into her hand.

qa.q: How much money had Vandana actually given?
qa.a: Fifty rupees.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when she looked at the coins for a long time?
qa.a: Vandana felt tempted and torn between keeping the money and being honest.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend who faces the same choice?
qa.a: Do what Vandana did: go back and return it, even if no one would find out.

qa.q: How might Pema aunty see Vandana after this?
qa.a: Pema aunty is grateful and will likely trust Vandana more, knowing she is honest even when unwatched.

grounding: A child returns extra change though no one would have known.

passage:
In the quiet street in Haifa, Yosef was kicking his ball against the wall. It bounced wrong and smashed the clay pot on Mr Daniel's step.
Nobody saw. Mr Daniel was at work. Yosef's heart thumped. He could just go inside.
He picked up the pieces and put them in a neat pile. Then he wrote a note: "Mr Daniel, I broke your pot with my ball. I'm sorry. I'll help you plant a new one. — Yosef, number 4."
In the evening, Mr Daniel knocked. Yosef's stomach dropped. But Mr Daniel held up the note. "This took courage." He smiled. "Saturday, then. Bring gloves."

qa.q: What did Yosef's ball smash?
qa.a: The clay pot on Mr Daniel's step.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling when his stomach dropped?
qa.a: Yosef felt nervous and afraid that Mr Daniel would be angry.

qa.q: What did Yosef's note do that just going inside would not?
qa.a: It admitted the mistake and offered to fix it, which built trust instead of hiding the harm.

qa.q: How does Mr Daniel see Yosef's note?
qa.a: Mr Daniel sees it as brave and honest, which matters more to him than the broken pot.

grounding: A child in Israel admits breaking a neighbour's pot though no one saw.

passage:
In the Class 6 classroom, the teacher had to leave for a meeting. "Swap and mark each other's spelling tests. Answers are on the board."
Damini marked Vandana's test and handed it back. Nine out of ten.
Vandana checked it. Her "necessary" had only one "s". Damini had missed it.
Nobody else would notice. The teacher would just copy the marks.
Vandana chewed her lip. Then she crossed out the tick, wrote eight, and walked to the teacher's desk when she came back. "It should be eight. Damini missed one."
Damini groaned. "You could've kept it!"
"I know," said Vandana.

qa.q: What mark did Damini give Vandana at first?
qa.a: Nine out of ten.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when she chewed her lip?
qa.a: Vandana felt tempted and uneasy, wanting the higher mark but knowing it wasn't honest.

qa.q: How could the teacher respond when Vandana corrects her mark?
qa.a: The teacher could thank her quietly for her honesty and show that it matters more than one mark.

qa.q: How does Damini see Vandana's choice?
qa.a: Damini is puzzled and a bit frustrated, because she thinks Vandana could easily have kept the mark.

grounding: A child corrects a marking error in her favour when no one would have noticed.

passage:
I'm Ayesha. I live on the floor above Karthik, and from our balcony you can see the whole courtyard.
Last Sunday evening Karthik was bouncing his cricket ball against the wall, alone. It flew sideways and knocked Mrs Pillai's tulsi pot off her ledge. The pot cracked. Nobody else was outside. I don't think he saw me.
He stood still for a long time. He even picked up the ball and walked toward his own door. Then he stopped, turned round, and rang Mrs Pillai's bell. I couldn't hear everything, but I saw him point at the pot and hold his hands out, like he was saying sorry. She put a hand on his head.
Next morning there was a new pot on the ledge, and Karthik was helping her replant the tulsi.

qa.q: What did Karthik's cricket ball knock off the ledge?
qa.a: The ball knocked Mrs Pillai's tulsi pot off her ledge, and the pot cracked.

qa.q: What might Karthik have been feeling while he stood still for a long time?
qa.a: Karthik was probably torn and worried, tempted to walk away since nobody saw, but uneasy about hiding what he did.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who breaks something when no one is watching?
qa.a: Tell the owner soon, say plainly what happened and offer to help fix it, the way Karthik helped replant the tulsi.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pillai see Karthik after he rang her bell?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai probably saw him as trustworthy and felt touched that he owned up, which is why she put a hand on his head instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a mistake when no one would have found out, as seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Monday, first rain of the monsoon. Siddharth got his maths test back: 18 out of 20. Walking home under Salma's umbrella, he checked it again and saw that question 7 was wrong but ticked. It should have been 16.
Wednesday. He hadn't told anyone. Salma said, "Teachers make mistakes, it's not your job to fix them." Siddharth laughed, but at night he kept opening his bag to look at the red tick. The 18 didn't feel like his.
Friday. He waited till the class emptied and showed Mr D'Souza the paper. "This one's wrong," he said, and his voice came out small.
Mr D'Souza changed the mark to 16, then wrote something beside it: "Honest. Thank you." Siddharth kept that page.

qa.q: Which question was marked wrongly on Siddharth's test?
qa.a: Question 7 was wrong but ticked, so the mark should have been 16, not 18.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth keep opening his bag to look at the red tick?
qa.a: Siddharth felt uneasy and guilty, because the 18 didn't feel like his own mark.

qa.q: How could a parent support a child in Siddharth's place on Wednesday?
qa.a: A parent could listen without scolding and help the child think through what would feel right, leaving the choice to tell the teacher with the child.

qa.q: What would change if Salma had found a wrong tick in Salma's own favour?
qa.a: Salma would face the same choice, and it might test whether Salma really believed fixing a teacher's mistake wasn't a student's job.

grounding: Illustrates a child choosing to report an in-their-favour marking error over several days, with no risk of being caught.

passage:
Payal, come sit, the Pongal rice can boil without us watching.
When I was about your age, in our village, Pongal meant new clay pots. My mother bought four and told me to carry them in from the cart. I carried three. The fourth slipped and broke into pieces behind the cowshed. Nobody saw. I buried the pieces under the hay.
That night Amma counted and said, "The potter must have cheated us." And she decided not to buy from him again. I lay awake feeling like a stone was on my chest. He was a poor man with a lame leg.
Next morning I dug up the pieces and showed her. She was angry for a while. Then she went and bought two more pots from him. I have never forgotten how light I felt after, Payal. That's why your Vasudha Paati always owns up first.

qa.q: Where did the young Vasudha hide the broken pieces?
qa.a: She buried the pieces under the hay behind the cowshed.

qa.q: Why did young Vasudha lie awake that night?
qa.a: Young Vasudha felt guilty and heavy, like a stone was on her chest, because the innocent potter was being blamed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Digging up the pieces the next morning mattered, because it stopped the potter losing a customer for something he didn't do.

qa.q: How was the potter affected by the girl's choice, even without knowing it?
qa.a: Her honesty saved his trade with the family; Amma bought two more pots from him instead of dropping him.

grounding: Shows an elder recounting how, as a child, she admitted a hidden accident because someone else was being blamed.

passage:
The rain was pouring and Irfan's mother had sent him to buy sugar before the Eid guests arrived. The shop was packed, and the shopkeeper, in a hurry, handed Irfan change for a five-hundred note. Irfan had given him a hundred.
Outside, under the awning, Irfan counted it twice. His friend Gurpreet whistled. "Lucky! He'll never know."
Irfan's heart was racing. Nobody had seen. The guests were coming. The rain was getting worse.
He went back in anyway, waited behind four people, and held out the extra notes. "Uncle, you gave me too much."
The shopkeeper stared, then laughed and gave Irfan a toffee. "Your parents raised you well."
Gurpreet shook his head, grinning. "Now I feel bad I said lucky."

qa.q: What note had Irfan given the shopkeeper?
qa.a: He had given him a hundred.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he counted the change?
qa.a: He felt nervous and tempted, his heart racing, knowing nobody had seen and he was in a hurry.

qa.q: Why was going back the right choice even though no one saw?
qa.a: Because the money wasn't his, and doing right when no one is watching is what makes a person trustworthy.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet feel after Irfan returns the money?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels a bit ashamed of calling it lucky, but also seems to admire his friend.

grounding: Shows a child being honest about a mistake in his favour even when nobody would find out.
